title: Plans, congratulations, and saying goodbye
goal: Talk about plans ahead, offer congratulations and blessings with the *-sin* form, use *oʻz* for "self", and say a warm goodbye.
bekal: making plans with the habitual form and *-moqchi*
offering blessings and congratulations: *Tugʻilgan kuningiz bilan!*, *Omad tilayman!*
using *oʻzim, oʻzingiz, oʻz uyim* to stress "myself" and "my own"

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Aeroportda xayrlashuv
dialogs.intro: Six months have passed. Budi is going back to Jakarta, and Nilufar and Anvar see him off at the airport.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.text: Ishonolmayapman — olti oy shunday tez oʻtdi.
lines.id: I can't believe it — six months went by so fast.
lines.literal: believe-can-not-I — six month so fast passed.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Men ham. Bu yerda oʻzimni uydagidek his qildim.
lines.id: Me neither. I felt right at home here.
lines.literal: I also. this place-in self-my-(object) home-in-like feeling did-I.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Of course. Next year I want to start a master's program.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.text: Zoʻr! Omad tilayman. Hamma ishingiz oʻngidan kelsin.
lines.id: Great! Good luck. May everything go well for you.
lines.literal: great! luck wish-I. all affair-your right-side-its-from let-come.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Rahmat. Sizlarsiz bu olti oy boshqacha boʻlardi.
lines.id: Thank you. Without you, these six months would have been different.
lines.literal: thanks. you-all-without this six month different would-be.

lines.speaker: Anvar:
lines.id: Here, a little gift. We picked it ourselves.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: A doppi! I'll show it to my family.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.text: Yangi yilingiz muborak boʻlsin, aytishni unutmang!
lines.id: Don't forget to wish them a happy New Year!
lines.literal: new year-your blessed let-be, saying-(object) don't-forget!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: I won't forget. Goodbye, my friends — see you!

lines.speaker: Anvar:
lines.id: Have a good trip! Get there safe and sound!

notes: **Oq yoʻl! literally means "white road"** and means "have a good trip". In Turkic culture white stands for purity and good fortune — as in *oq fotiha* (the parents' blessing before a wedding).

**Hamma ishingiz oʻngidan kelsin** literally means "may all your affairs come from the right side". An everyday wish for things to go smoothly. The *-sin* form is a command for the third person: "may it…".
**Uydagidek = "like at home".** Three endings stacked up: *uy* + *-da* (at) + *-gi* (the one that is) + *-dek* (like). Uzbek builds a word this long from pieces you already know.
**Boʻlardi = "would be" (hypothetical).** A form for something that didn't actually happen, like English "would have". It's on the edge of A2; just learn this phrase whole.

grammars.title: Oʻz: oneself, one's own
body: *Oʻz* covers two things English handles separately: "-self" for emphasis, and "own" for possession.
after: As an object, it takes *-ni* like any noun: *oʻzimni* (myself), *oʻzingizni* (yourself). *Oʻzingizni ehtiyot qiling* = "take good care of yourself".
*Oʻz* in front of a noun is always followed by a possessive ending: *oʻz uyim*, *oʻz ishingiz*, *oʻz fikri*. *Oʻz* without the possessive ending sounds unfinished.
Some phrases worth learning whole: *oʻzi haqida* (about himself/herself), *oʻz-oʻzidan* (by itself), *oʻzbekcha aytganda* (as they say in Uzbek).

grammars.title: -sin and tilamoq: offering blessings
body: Uzbek is very rich in everyday blessings. The two tools are simple, and once you have them, dozens of phrases open up.
after: *Muborak* is the Arabic *mubarak* (blessed), and the pattern *… muborak boʻlsin* is used for every celebration: *Yangi yilingiz muborak boʻlsin!*, *Navroʻzingiz muborak!*
The pattern *… bilan!* (literally "with …") is the shortest way to congratulate someone: *Bayram bilan!* (happy holiday), *Yangi yil bilan!* (happy New Year).
⚠️ *Sogʻ boʻling* has two jobs: a wish for good health, and a thank-you warmer than *rahmat*. If someone helps you, it's the reply people like most.

blocks.text: Uzbekistan's biggest holiday isn't January 1st but *Navroʻz* — the Persian New Year on March 21, celebrated by cooking *sumalak* all night long in a huge cauldron.

⚠️ Two goodbyes you mustn't mix up: the one **leaving** says *Yaxshi qoling!* ("stay well"), and the one **staying** replies *Yaxshi boring!* ("go well"). English just says "goodbye" both ways; Uzbek, like many languages, marks who is going.
*Hayit* is the same word as Arabic *Eid*. In Uzbekistan the two Eids are called *Roʻza hayiti* (Eid al-Fitr, "the fasting feast") and *Qurbon hayiti* (Eid al-Adha). Both are national holidays.
A1 Uzbek has no separate future form. Instead you use two forms you've already mastered, plus a time expression.
Time words to go with them: *kelasi hafta* (next week), *kelasi oy*, *kelasi yil*, *keyingi safar* (next time), *yaqinda* (soon), *bir kun* (one day).

And one closing sentence worth taking with you: *Bir kun yana Oʻzbekistonga qaytaman* — "one day I'll come back to Uzbekistan". If you've made it to this page, you can already say it, understand every ending in it, and explain why the verb stands at the end.
